children: By Eric Onstad

North American rare earth recycling company Cyclic Materials has taken a step towards establishing operations in Europe, ahead of expansion in Asia in the coming years, CEO Ahmad Ghahreman told Reuters.
The private company  —  backed by investors including Microsoft
, Amazon
and BMW
—  aims to supply markets in the West where governments are trying to cut dependence on China, which produces 90% of global processed rare earths.
Cyclic has secured a site in Germany to extract rare earth permanent magnets from discarded products, the first of five such sites it plans to build in the region, Ghahreman said in an interview.
"Europe is critical for us... and at a point in the future Asia, ex-China, will be as well," he said.
The company launched operations in September at a facility in Arizona, which can process up to 25,000 metric tons annually of scrap material such as computer hard drives, electric motors and drones.
The facility in the central German town of Schkopau, near Leipzig, will have similar processing capacity when it launches operations in 2028, Ghahreman said.
Asked if the company would go public, he said it was well financed and had multiple options for further capitalisation.
NO GOVERNMENT PRICE SUPPORT
Some rare earths miners, including MP Materials
, have received support from the US government, which has guaranteed a minimum price for production of two rare earths.
Ghahreman said Cyclic did not need such support.
"We are not asking our customers to pay a premium, simply because our cost of production is less than the market price," he said.
"Our cost of production is less than many of the mining projects outside China."
He said one reason Cyclic's cost structure is low is that it recovers other metals from scrap and not just rare earth magnets.

About 25,000 tons of scrap yields about 225 tons of rare earth oxides, 14,000 tons of steel, 4,600 tons of aluminium and 3,000 tons of copper. The non-rare earth metals comprise 40% to 50% of Cyclic's revenue, Ghahreman said.
Under the company's "spoke and hub" structure, five plants handling scrap will feed one chemical processing facility where old magnet material is refined and separated into rare earth oxides.
